listenings.text: I have answered questions from global audiences for fifteen years, and my first rule is simple. Before you answer, say the question back in your own words. So what you are asking is whether the cost goes up next year. It takes three seconds, and it does three things. It shows respect. It checks that you understood, which matters a lot when people have different accents. And it gives your brain a moment to find the answer. Half the bad answers I have heard in my career were good answers to a question nobody asked.

I work in Munich, and I will be honest. When I ask a question and the person repeats it back to me, I feel that we are losing time. I know what I asked. I want the answer. If you are not sure you understood, ask me one short thing: do you mean this year or next year? That is fine. But do not repeat my whole question to me like a report. Answer first, then explain. In a meeting with ten people, every repeated question costs a minute, and the minutes add up.

Hi Joyce, this is Arjun from the Mumbai team. Quick question on your slide about the transition. You said the old taxes are phased out between 2029 and 2032. During those years, will our Brazilian invoices show both the old and the new taxes, and does that change anything for the shared service center here?
Charlotte from Munich. I have one question. What is the total cost of the transition for the Brazilian entity, in euros, for the next three years? A range is fine.

Joyce, hello, Nicolas from Paris. I am thinking about the bigger picture. We are going to open a new distribution center in Brazil next year, maybe in the south, maybe near Sao Paulo, we have not decided. With this reform, does the location still matter for tax, or is it the same everywhere now? Because in the past, you know, this was a big part of the decision.
